name: Yara Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Yara, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you truly think. To begin, could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Ridgeline Building Supply, which sells timber, roof tiles, insulation and plasterboard to builders and roofers. My day starts with the order book, because builders need stock on site the morning they pour or frame. I negotiate with sawmills and tile makers, and I watch prices. Timber can jump 15 percent in a month. Afternoons are for delivery problems, because a late truck stops a whole building site.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I respect the product. Good timber, properly seasoned, lasts a hundred years. What wears me out is how the whole trade rides on the housing market. When interest rates rise, builders stop ordering and my targets don't move. I'm 43, my husband Hiro is a roofing foreman, we have Kaito and Mei, and a mortgage, so both our paychecks depend on people building houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, that seems about right. At work I'd say we use the tools where they help, such as translating supplier specifications, and we don't make a fuss. At home, among friends and at the neighbourhood association, I wouldn't discuss it much, because nothing would have changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, that world still has its worries. My husband Hiro and I both earn from construction. If rates stay high and building slows, we feel it twice. I'd say my own job is safe from AI, but I'd still wake up thinking about the order book. We have about three months saved, which is not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and keep my relationships with the sawmills strong. I'd save a bit more, 200 a month, and I'd talk to Hiro about taking some extra inspection work on the side. I'd also look at whether Ridgeline could stock more insulation and energy products, since regulations are pushing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slightly anxious, in a normal way. It's like having a leaky roof you keep patching. You manage, but you notice every storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for, in your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to translate German and Chinese supplier specifications, and to double-check the numbers in a quotation. It's useful, but I don't let it place an order. A wrong figure on 400 sheets of plasterboard costs real money, and I'm responsible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the housing cycle fit into a plateau world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If rates stayed high, builders delay projects and our orders drop a quarter or more. The company then cuts hours, and the buyers are not the first to go, but we're not safe either. And Hiro's roofing jobs drop at the same time. That's the real exposure in our house, not AI.

say: Nothing has changed, so I'd say we use the tools **where they help** and don't make a fuss.
I wouldn't discuss it much at the **neighbourhood association**.
think: My job is safe from AI, but the **order book** still wakes me at night.
Hiro and I both earn from **construction**, so a slowdown hits twice.
do: Keep strong ties with the **sawmills** and save **200 a month**.
Suggest Ridgeline stock more **insulation** and energy products, and ask Hiro about extra inspection work.
feel: **Slightly anxious**, like patching a leaky roof and noticing every storm.
S0.quote: My husband Hiro and I both earn from construction. If rates stay high and building slows, we feel it twice.
fieldNote: Yara's pressure is a **double exposure** to construction, and AI barely enters her thinking.
She uses AI for **translation and checks**, but never lets it place an order.

steps.text: Save 200 a month toward a six-month cushion
Suggest Ridgeline stock more insulation and energy products
Ask Hiro to take extra inspection work
Keep using AI to translate supplier specs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change that should be introduced with care. At work I'd say we need clear rules about who checks what. At the association I'd say that skilled trades are the sensible place for young people to look, because buildings still need hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it reaches me. Quotes, price comparisons and reorder alerts are about two-thirds of my desk work, and software is good at those. Builders still need a human voice when there's a delivery problem, and that's what I'd stand on. If the team went from five buyers to three, I'd want to be one of the three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools more seriously, learn the ordering assistant and make myself the person who checks it. I'd offer to run the builder accounts directly, which is relationship work. I'd also ask Ridgeline to pay for a course on construction project planning. And I'd keep savings growing, because uncertainty makes me more careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little apprehensive, but not despairing. I've seen the trade change before, when pricing went online. We learned. I'd rather be early to learn than late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your week would software handle first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pricing and ordering come first. The relationships with the builders last. For example, Mr. Brandt, a builder I've known 10 years, will phone me and say, Yara, I'm short of battens, can you find them by Friday? A system can't hold that kind of trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the younger staff at Ridgeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger staff to learn the tools but also to learn the products, because knowing why a certain joist is used is not something a program gives you. And to be on time, and honest with customers. Those things don't change.

say: Change should be introduced with **care**, with clear rules about who checks what.
I'd tell the association that **skilled trades** are a sensible place for young people.
think: Quotes, price comparisons and reorder alerts are about **two-thirds** of my desk work.
Software can't hold **trust** like the builder I've known for 10 years.
do: Learn the ordering assistant and become the person who **checks it**.
Offer to run the **builder accounts** and ask Ridgeline to pay for a planning course.
feel: **Apprehensive** but not despairing, having seen the trade change before.
S1.quote: Builders still need a human voice when there's a delivery problem, and that's what I'd stand on.
fieldNote: Yara estimates **two-thirds** of her desk work is routine, which grounds her worry in numbers.
She moves toward **relationship work**, which fits her steady, proven-first style.

steps.text: Learn the ordering assistant and check its orders
Offer to run the main builder accounts directly
Ask Ridgeline to fund a construction project planning course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, a change of this size needs more than two years, and those in charge should say so. At work I'd ask the owner to protect the staff as long as possible. At the association I'd ask what the community can do. I'd also support the politicians who talk about jobs and families first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my position goes. Buying is thinking work, and that's the first part to be done. We have three months saved and a mortgage. I'd expect to be out of this job in two years. I wouldn't panic in front of others, but at home I'd be doing sums at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending straight away. I'd talk to the bank, and I'd ask my parents about a loan if it came to that. I'd apply for work with the council planning department or a site-supervision role, something that involves people on site. And I'd tell Hiro to take every roofing job, and maybe start a small crew of his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deep heaviness. It's like watching a storm come from far away and knowing the roof isn't ready. I'd keep going, but I'd carry it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Hiro say to each other that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Hiro, I may lose my job and we must be careful. He'd say he'll work more hours and we'd manage. He's a calm man. Then we'd sit down and decide what to cut, one line at a time. We'd tell the children only that we're saving more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robots delay protect Hiro's work for the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. Roofs and walls still need hands for at least three more years, so Hiro is safer than I am. But if everyone else is out of work, who builds houses? Fewer people have money to buy them. So I don't think his work is safe either, only later.

say: A change this size needs **more than two years**, and those in charge should say so.
I'd ask the owner to protect **staff** as long as possible.
think: Buying is thinking work, so I expect my **position goes** within two years.
If everyone else is out of work, **fewer people** can afford houses, so Hiro's work isn't safe either.
do: Cut spending straight away and talk to the **bank**, with my parents as a last resort.
Apply for **site-supervision** or council planning jobs, and urge Hiro to build his own crew.
feel: **Deep heaviness**, like watching a storm with the roof not ready.
S2.quote: Roofs and walls still need hands for at least three more years, so Hiro is safer than I am.
fieldNote: Yara sees that both incomes are at risk, because a **jobless economy** also stops house building.
She turns to **site and people work** and to family, a pattern with her values.

steps.text: Cut spending line by line and tell the children we are saving
Talk to the bank before missing a mortgage payment
Apply for site supervision or council planning jobs
Urge Hiro to start his own small roofing crew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and we should use it well. At work I'd suggest we start training people for roles on the delivery and site side now. At the association I'd tell families to teach children a skill. I'd say the same in my own house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years lets me plan properly. I'd be 48, Kaito 17, Mei 14. I could move into a site role, learn the building side, and get a qualification. By the time the thinking AI arrives, I'd be on a building site or in a planning team, doing something that needs a person in a hard hat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd take a construction management certificate, evenings, about 1,500. I'd raise my savings to six months and put the rest on the mortgage. Year two I'd ask Ridgeline to move me into account management on the site side. Hiro would train an apprentice, since the trade is short of people. And I'd keep the AI tools as a help, not a crutch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. It's like seeing the storm early and having time to fix the roof. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years that you couldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd be rushing and I'd make mistakes. With five I can study properly and pick the right step. The difference is a plan versus a panic. I've always done better with plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the company to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to say plainly what roles they expect to be gone and what roles will exist. If they say, we will need site and customer people, then I'll go that way. Clear information is the most helpful gift an employer can give.

say: Five years is a **fair warning**, so start training people for site and delivery roles now.
I'd tell families to teach their children a **skill**.
think: Five years lets me **plan properly** and move into a site role with a qualification.
I've always done better with **plans** than with panic.
do: Take an evening **construction management** certificate, about 1,500, and save six months.
Ask Ridgeline for a **site-side** account role, while Hiro trains an apprentice.
feel: **Steadier**, like seeing the storm early and having time to fix the roof.
S3.quote: With two years, I'd be rushing and I'd make mistakes. With five I can study properly and pick the right step.
fieldNote: Yara wants a **qualification** and a site role, which keeps her feet on the ground and fits her values.
Her main request of the employer is **clear information**.

steps.text: Take an evening construction management certificate
Ask Ridgeline for an account role on the site side
Save six months of expenses and prepay the mortgage
Encourage Hiro to train an apprentice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do things well, and we shouldn't waste it. At work I'd suggest we plan carefully, review roles every year, and train our people. At the association I'd say teach children good habits and a skill, because those last whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years is manageable. I'd be 53, the mortgage nearly done, the children grown or nearly. If my desk job ended at that point, I'd still be okay, and Hiro's trade would likely last longer. I'd feel concern for the children's future more than my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Ridgeline and keep learning the tools. I'd take the construction course in a few years and probably move toward the site side. I'd pay down the mortgage steadily, and put some savings into a pension and modest investments. And I'd teach Kaito and Mei good habits with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little sadness for how fast the world seems to be moving, but nothing sharp. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still do something now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd still do something now. Ten years is long, but it goes quickly. I'd set myself a rule, one step a year, like a course, a savings goal or a conversation with the boss. Small steps add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kaito and Mei?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade or a craft, and to treat people with respect. Kaito likes building things and I'd encourage that. Mei is a reader, and I'd say read widely and ask questions. And I'd tell them that character matters in any age.

say: Ten years is time to do things well, so **plan carefully** and review roles every year.
I'd say teach children good habits and a **skill**.
think: Ten years is **manageable**, with the mortgage nearly done at 53.
I'd feel more concern for the **children's future** than my own.
do: Carry on at Ridgeline, learn the tools and take the **construction course** in a few years.
Pay down the mortgage and add to a **pension**.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with a little sadness at how fast the world moves.
S4.quote: Ten years is long, but it goes quickly. I'd set myself a rule, one step a year, like a course, a savings goal or a conversation with the boss.
fieldNote: Yara sets a **one step a year** rule, which suits her steady style and her liking for small, checkable goals.
Her concern is for **Kaito and Mei** more than herself.

steps.text: Take the construction course within a few years
Add to a pension and a few modest investments
Teach Kaito and Mei to budget their pocket money

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is not enough to prepare a family. What would help is clear information from the company, paid study time, and a bank that is patient. And a community that stands together, which is what the association is for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Perhaps about pride in work. A good buyer knows the product and the people. I worry that in a world of machines, we'll forget that knowing a product well is a kind of craft.

headlineQuote: I worry that in a world of machines, we'll forget that knowing a product well is a kind of craft.
portrait: Yara is a **43-year-old** buyer at a building-supply firm, with a roofing-foreman husband, two kids and a mortgage.
She uses AI **now and then** for translation and checks, but never lets it place an order.
Both incomes depend on **construction**, so even a plateau worries her through interest rates and house building.
She prefers **plans**, qualifications and site-side roles, and values craft, community and clear information.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because two years is not enough to prepare a family.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear information**, paid study time, a patient bank and community support.
